title: CATARACT 2, MULTIPLE TYPES
alt_titles: CATARACT 2, MULTIPLE TYPES, WITH OR WITHOUT MICROCORNEA

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that multiple types of cataract (CTRCT2), with or without microcornea, are caused by heterozygous mutation in the gamma-C-crystallin gene (CRYGC) on chromosome 2q33-q35.

checks.claim: Multiple types of cataract (CTRCT2), with or without microcornea, are caused by heterozygous mutation in the gamma-C-crystallin gene (CRYGC).
checks.evidence_quote: Further analysis of the original Coppock-like-cataract family identified a missense mutation in a highly conserved segment of exon 2 of CRYGC.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports CRYGC mutation causing Coppock-like cataract. It does not mention heterozygosity, microcornea or multiple cataract types (abstract only).

checks.claim: The CRYGC gene is located on chromosome 2q33-q35.
checks.evidence_quote: We have localized the cataracts to a 19-cM interval on chromosome 2q33-q35 including the gamma-crystallin gene cluster.
checks.explanation: The gamma-crystallin cluster, which includes CRYGC, lies within the 2q33-q35 interval.

paragraphs.text: CRYGC-related cataract is an autosomal dominant congenital lens opacity. The papers describe several morphologic types: Coppock-like cataract of the embryonic nucleus, variable zonular pulverulent cataract, lamellar cataract, and nuclear cataract. Some families also have microcornea (Heon et al., 1999; Ren et al., 2000; Gonzalez-Huerta et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2009).

paragraphs.text: Scott et al. (1994) described a 7-generation family in which 48 of 138 individuals were known to have autosomal dominant congenital pulverulent cataracts. Of 53 individuals examined, 28 had congenital cataracts: 19 unilateral (8 right eyes and 11 left eyes) and 9 bilateral. In patients with unilateral cataract, detailed slit-lamp examination showed no lens opacity in the clinically unaffected eye. Severity ranged from a subtle unilateral zonular cataract with 20/20 visual acuity, to bilateral inner fetal nuclear pulverulent opacities with 20/16 visual acuity in both eyes, to dense unilateral and bilateral nuclear cataracts that required early surgical removal. Counting historical data on unexamined members, there were 48 affected members: 28 unilateral, 17 bilateral, and 3 unexamined obligate carriers. The authors noted that hereditary cataracts are typically symmetric, so this apparently random unilateral or bilateral expression was unusual.

paragraphs.text: Zhang et al. (2009) studied a 4-generation Chinese family from a relatively isolated region of northern China, in which 6 members had congenital nuclear cataracts and microcornea. Affected individuals had bilateral central nuclear opacities involving the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nucleus of the lens. They also had congenitally small eyeballs and corneas about 9 to 10 mm in diameter. Every affected individual had visual acuity of hand movements, together with nystagmus and amblyopia. There were no other ocular or systemic abnormalities.

paragraphs.text: Guo et al. (2012) described a 4-generation Chinese family in which 6 members had isolated bilateral nuclear cataracts and microcornea. The opacities involved the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nuclei, and corneal diameter was approximately 9 mm. Age at diagnosis ranged from 6 months to 13 years. The proband was diagnosed at age 8 years and had a best corrected visual acuity of 0.08 in the right eye. All patients had nystagmus and amblyopia, and intraocular pressure was normal.

paragraphs.text: Lubsen et al. Every affected family member carried it. The cataract locus was closely linked to the gamma-crystallin gene cluster, with a maximum lod score of 7.58 at theta = 0.

paragraphs.text: Heon et al. (1999) found that the sequence changes in the CRYGE pseudogene, previously proposed as the cause of Coppock-like cataract, were a polymorphism present in 23% of their control population. On further analysis of the original Coppock-like cataract family (Lubsen et al., 1987), they identified a missense mutation in CRYGC, in a highly conserved segment of exon 2. The mutation was not found in a large control population. Zhang et al. (2009) and Guo et al. (2012) later listed this mutation as thr5-to-pro (T5P), and Guo et al. (2012) gave its nucleotide change as c.13A-C.

paragraphs.text: In the family with variable autosomal dominant zonular pulverulent cataract reported by Scott et al. (1994), Ren et al. (2000) sequenced the CRYGC and CRYGD genes. CRYGD was normal. In every affected family member they found a heterozygous 5-bp duplication in exon 2 of CRYGC, which was absent from unaffected family members and controls. The duplication disrupts the reading frame and is predicted to produce an unstable gamma-C-crystallin made up of 38 amino acids of the first Greek key motif followed by 52 random amino acids. Ren et al. (2000) also found that the pseudo-gamma-E-crystallin promoter sequence made activation of the pseudogene an unlikely cause of cataract in this family. TATA-box changes were found in unaffected controls.

paragraphs.text: In a family with primary congenital nuclear cataract, Gonzalez-Huerta et al. (2007) sequenced the CRYGA-CRYGD gene cluster and found a heterozygous c.502C-T transition in CRYGC, resulting in an arg168-to-trp (R168W) substitution. The mutation segregated with the disease and was not found in healthy family members or in 170 unrelated controls. The authors noted that this mutation had previously been associated with lamellar cataract but was listed as a SNP in the NCBI database. They concluded that R168W is disease-causing and that it shows phenotypic heterogeneity.

paragraphs.text: In a 4-generation Chinese family with congenital nuclear cataracts and microcornea, Zhang et al. (2009) identified a heterozygous c.470G-A change in exon 3 of CRYGC, predicted to produce a trp157-to-ter (W157X) substitution at a phylogenetically conserved residue. The mutation cosegregated with the disease and was not found in 100 normal controls. It was predicted to truncate 17 C-terminal amino acids and to disrupt the fourth Greek key motif.

paragraphs.text: In a 3-generation Chinese family with autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataract, Li et al. (2012) sequenced candidate genes and identified a heterozygous c.385G-T mutation in CRYGC, resulting in a gly129-to-cys (G129C) substitution at a highly conserved residue. In molecular modeling and spectroscopic studies, the mutation impaired the protein's tertiary structure by altering the hydrogen-bonding network in the C-terminal domain. The mutant protein had greatly reduced thermal stability. It was also much more prone to aggregate at high concentrations and under heat and UV-irradiation stress.

paragraphs.text: In a 4-generation Chinese family with congenital nuclear cataracts and microcornea, Guo et al. (2012) screened 9 candidate genes. They identified a heterozygous c.471G-A transition (TGG-to-TGA) in exon 3 of CRYGC, predicted to cause a trp157-to-ter (W157X) substitution. The mutation cosegregated with the disease and was not found in 100 ethnically matched controls. This was the same protein change reported by Zhang et al. (2009), but caused by a different nucleotide substitution. Guo et al. (2012) noted that the phenotypes of the 2 families were similar.

paragraphs.text: Brakenhoff et al. (1994) cloned the CRYGD and pseudo-gamma-E (CRYGE) genes from the Coppock-like cataract chromosome in the family reported by Lubsen et al. (1987). The CRYGD gene was functionally equivalent to its wildtype allele. The CRYGE pseudogene, however, had a cluster of sequence changes within and around its TATA box. Together these changes increased promoter activity 10-fold, raising CRYGE expression to 30% of that of CRYGD. The authors proposed that reactivation of the pseudogene, with overexpression of a predicted 6-kD N-terminal gamma-crystallin fragment, could cause the cataract. Heon et al. (1999) later found that these CRYGE changes were a polymorphism present in 23% of controls. They identified a CRYGC missense mutation in the original family and noted that there was no direct evidence that upregulation of a pseudogene causes cataract.

checks.claim: Brakenhoff et al. (1994) cloned the CRYGD and pseudo-gamma-E (CRYGE) genes from the Coppock-like cataract chromosome in the family reported by Lubsen et al. (1987).
checks.evidence_quote: The gamma D and the psi gamma E gene were cloned from the CCL chromosome and characterized.
checks.explanation: The cloning of both genes from the CCL chromosome is supported. The abstract does not name the family, so the link to the family reported by Lubsen et al. (1987) cannot be confirmed from the abstract alone.

checks.claim: Brakenhoff et al. (1994) found that the CRYGD gene from the Coppock-like cataract chromosome was functionally equivalent to its wildtype allele.
checks.evidence_quote: The gamma D gene was functionally equivalent to its allele cloned from a wild-type chromosome.

checks.evidence_quote: raising the level of expression of this gene to 30% of that of the gamma D gene.

checks.evidence_quote: The predicted protein product of the psi gamma E gene is a 6 kD N-terminal gamma-crystallin fragment. Reactivation of the psi gamma E gene and concomitant overexpression of the gamma-crystallin fragment could be the cause of the Coppock-like cataract.

checks.evidence_quote: There is no direct evidence, to date, that up-regulation of a pseudogene causes cataracts.

paragraphs.text: In the original family with Coppock-like cataract of the embryonic lens nucleus (Lubsen et al., 1987), Heon et al. (1999) identified a missense mutation in a highly conserved segment of exon 2 of the CRYGC gene. The mutation was not found in a large control population. Zhang et al. (2009) and Guo et al. (2012) listed it as a thr5-to-pro (T5P) substitution, and Guo et al. (2012) gave the nucleotide change as c.13A-C.

paragraphs.text: In a 7-generation family with variable autosomal dominant zonular pulverulent cataract (Scott et al., 1994), Ren et al. (2000) found a 5-bp duplication in exon 2 of the CRYGC gene on 1 allele in every affected family member. It was absent from unaffected family members and unaffected controls. The duplication disrupts the reading frame and is predicted to produce an unstable protein made up of 38 amino acids of the first Greek key motif followed by 52 random amino acids. Guo et al. (2012) listed this mutation as c.123-128insGCGGC.

checks.evidence_quote: The authors describe a seven-generation family with 48 of 138 individuals known to be affected with autosomal dominant congenital cataracts of the pulverulent type.
checks.explanation: The 7-generation autosomal dominant family with pulverulent cataract and variable expression is supported. The abstract does not describe the cataract as 'zonular pulverulent' overall; only one zonular case is mentioned.

checks.claim: Ren et al. (2000) found a 5-bp duplication in exon 2 of the CRYGC gene on 1 allele in every affected member of the zonular pulverulent cataract family.
checks.evidence_quote: a 5-bp duplication within exon 2 of the gammaC-crystallin gene has been found in one allele of each affected family member

checks.evidence_quote: is predicted to result in the synthesis of an unstable gammaC-crystallin with 38 amino acids of the first "Greek key" motif followed by 52 random amino acids.

paragraphs.text: In a family with primary congenital nuclear cataract, Gonzalez-Huerta et al. (2007) identified a heterozygous c.502C-T transition in the CRYGC gene, resulting in an arg168-to-trp (R168W) substitution. The mutation segregated with the disease and was absent from healthy family members and from 170 unrelated controls. The authors noted that the mutation had previously been associated with lamellar cataract but was listed as a SNP in the NCBI database. They concluded that R168W is disease-causing.

checks.explanation: The variant, its zygosity and the amino acid change all match; the family's cataract is nuclear.

checks.claim: The CRYGC R168W mutation segregated with the disease in the Gonzalez-Huerta et al. (2007) family.
checks.evidence_quote: we described a family with nuclear congenital cataract that segregated the CRYGC missense mutation c.502C>T.
checks.explanation: The abstract states that the mutation segregated with the disease.

checks.claim: The CRYGC R168W mutation was absent from healthy family members and from 170 unrelated controls.

checks.evidence_quote: Our data and previous report support that R168W is the actual disease-causing mutation and should no longer be considered a SNP.
